questions.question: Integer demand $D\ge0$ has CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$; underage cost $b>0$, overage cost $h>0$, $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, and the expected cost $G(y)$ of ordering $y$ satisfies $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$. Over whole-number order quantities $y$, which $y$ is the smallest order quantity with the lowest expected cost?
options: The largest $y$ with $F(y)<\beta$
The smallest $y$ with $F(y)\ge\beta$
The $y$ whose value $F(y)$ is closest to $\beta$
The smallest $y$ with $\mathbb{P}(D=y)\ge\beta$

questions.question: Demand $D$ for a newsvendor takes nonnegative integer values with CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$; the underage cost is $b>0$, the overage cost $h>0$, and $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. Moving from $y$ to $y+1$ units changes the expected cost by $G(y+1)-G(y)=h\,F(y)-b\,(1-F(y))$. What does the term $b\,(1-F(y))$ measure?
options: The expected loss if the extra unit ends up unsold
The expected margin earned on all units that sell
The probability that the extra unit will be sold
The expected lost margin avoided by the extra unit

questions.question: Integer demand $D\ge0$ has CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$; underage cost $b>0$, overage cost $h>0$, $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, and the expected cost $G(y)$ of ordering $y$ satisfies $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$. Why may one stop at the first $y$ with $F(y)\ge\beta$, without checking larger $y$?
options: $F$ never decreases, so once a difference is $\ge0$, later ones are too.
$G$ decreases in $y$, so the first crossing point is its lowest value.
Demand never exceeds the first $y$ with $F(y)\ge\beta$, so more is waste.
Since $\beta<1$, the differences can change sign at most at one $y$.

questions.question: Demand $D$ for a newsvendor takes nonnegative integer values with CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$; the underage cost is $b>0$, the overage cost $h>0$, and $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. A newsvendor already holds $y$ units and adds one more, the $(y+1)$-th. For which demand values is this extra unit left over at the end of the period?
options: When $D\le y+1$, so demand does not exceed the new stock
When $D<y$, so demand stays below the old stock
When $D\le y$, so the first $y$ units cover all demand
When $D\ge y+1$, so demand reaches the new stock level

questions.question: Integer demand $D\ge0$ has CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$; underage cost $b>0$, overage cost $h>0$, $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, and the expected cost $G(y)$ of ordering $y$ satisfies $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$. Which condition does every whole-number order quantity $y$ that gives the lowest expected cost satisfy (taking $F(-1)=0$)?
options: $F(y-1)\le\beta\le F(y)$
$F(y)\le\beta\le F(y+1)$
$F(y)=\beta$ exactly
$F(y)\ge\beta$ only

questions.question: Integer demand has CDF values $F(2)=0.10$, $F(3)=0.30$, $F(4)=0.55$, $F(5)=0.78$, $F(6)=0.92$, $F(7)=1$ (and $F(1)=0$). The underage cost is $b=4$ and the overage cost $h=1$, so $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. Which smallest whole-number order gives the lowest expected cost?

Daily demand is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 with probabilities 0.05, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.05. The underage cost is $b=3$ and the overage cost $h=7$, so $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. Which smallest whole-number order gives the lowest expected cost?

For an integer-demand newsvendor with underage cost $b=6$ and overage cost $h=2$, the expected cost $G$ satisfies $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$, where $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$. At the current order $y$, $F(y)=0.7$. What does one more unit do to $G$?
options: It raises $G$ by $0.4$
It lowers $G$ by $4.6$
It lowers $G$ by $0.4$
It raises $G$ by $1.4$

questions.question: Daily demand is 0, 1, 2 or 3 units with probabilities 0.45, 0.1, 0.15, 0.3. The underage cost is $b=2$ and the overage cost $h=3$, so $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. Which whole-number order gives the lowest expected cost?

Demand is 2, 4 or 6 units with probabilities 0.3, 0.5, 0.2. A newsvendor orders $y=4$; each leftover unit costs $h=2$ and each unit short costs $b=5$. What is the expected cost $G(4)=h\,\mathbb{E}[(4-D)^+]+b\,\mathbb{E}[(D-4)^+]$?

Integer demand $D\ge0$ has CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$; underage cost $b>0$, overage cost $h>0$, $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, and the expected cost $G(y)$ of ordering $y$ satisfies $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$. Here $\beta=0.7$, $F(4)=0.69$ and $F(5)=0.95$. A planner orders 4, as $F(4)$ is far closer to $\beta$ than $F(5)$. Which assessment is right?
options: Ordering 4 is right, as $F(4)$ is the value closest to $\beta$
Orders 4 and 5 tie, as $F(4)$ lies within 0.01 of $\beta$
Ordering 5 is better, as $F$ should be as close to 1 as possible
Ordering 5 is better, as $G(5)-G(4)=(b+h)(F(4)-\beta)<0$ here

questions.question: Products X and Y have the same underage cost $b$ and overage cost $h$, integer demand, and the same smallest optimal order $y^*=10$ (so the same $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$), with $G$ the expected cost $h\,\mathbb{E}[(y-D)^+]+b\,\mathbb{E}[(D-y)^+]$. Which statement about their expected costs at 10 is correct?
options: They are equal, since $b$, $h$ and $y^*$ all agree
They can differ, since $G$ depends on the whole pmf
They equal $b\,(1-\beta)$, the margin left at risk
They are equal, since $G$ is set by $\frac{b}{b+h}$

questions.question: Integer demand is 3, 4, 5, 6 or 8 with probabilities 0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.2; with $b=3$, $h=2$ and $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}=0.6$ the smallest optimal order is $y^*=5$. The 0.2 probability at 8 is moved to 30, all else unchanged. What happens to $y^*$ and to the expected cost $G(y^*)$?
options: $y^*$ stays 5 and $G(5)$ rises
$y^*$ rises and $G(5)$ is unchanged
$y^*$ stays 5 and $G(5)$ is unchanged
$y^*$ falls and $G(5)$ rises

questions.question: For an integer-demand newsvendor with $b=9$, $h=1$ and $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}=0.9$, the smallest optimal order $y^*$ has $F(y^*-1)=0.5$ and $F(y^*)=0.95$, where $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$ and $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$. How much higher is $G(y^*-1)$ than $G(y^*)$?

A stall sells at $p=20$ an item bought at $c=12$; each leftover costs 4 to dispose of, so $s=-4$. Integer demand has $F(10)=0.10$, $F(11)=0.30$, $F(12)=0.36$, $F(13)=0.45$, $F(14)=0.70$, $F(15)=0.90$, $F(16)=1$. With $b=p-c$, $h=c-s$ and $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, which smallest whole-number order gives the lowest expected cost?

Integer demand is 5, 6, 7 or 8 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5, 0.15, 0.1; $b=3$, $h=1$, $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$, and expected cost satisfies $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$. What is $G(7)-G(6)$, and what does it imply?
options: $0$: orders 6 and 7 have the same cost
$0.6$: the seventh unit adds expected cost
$-0.75$: ordering 7 is strictly better
$0.75$: only an order of 6 is optimal

questions.question: Integer demand $D\ge0$ has CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$; underage cost $b>0$, overage cost $h>0$, $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, and the expected cost $G(y)$ of ordering $y$ satisfies $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$. A planner orders the smallest $y$ with $F(y)>\beta$ (strict) instead of $F(y)\ge\beta$. How does this variant perform?
options: It can stop at a quantity with higher expected cost
It is always optimal; it differs only at an exact tie
It always gives the same order as the usual rule
It is optimal only when every $F(y)$ differs from $\beta$

questions.question: Integer demand $D$ has CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$ with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=0.1$. A product is sold at its unit cost, so the underage cost is $b=p-c=0$, while leftovers lose $h>0$ each; $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$ and $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$. Which whole-number order gives the lowest expected cost?
options: The median demand, since $\beta=0$ removes the trade-off
The largest demand, since shortages now cost nothing
None, since $\beta=0$ is outside the range $0<\beta<1$
Zero, since each extra unit changes cost by $hF(y)>0$

questions.question: Integer demand is 5, 6, 8 or 9 units with probabilities 0.25, 0.5, 0.15, 0.1 (demand 7 never occurs); $b=3$, $h=1$, $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$, and $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$ for expected cost $G$. Which whole-number orders give the lowest $G$?
options: 6 only
6 and 7
6, 7 and 8

questions.question: Integer demand is 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1; $b=4$, $h=1$, $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$ and $G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b$ for expected cost $G$. A manager orders the most likely demand, 3. By how much would the optimal order lower expected cost?
